tags.gist: Would keep the risk-proportionate direction but extend it to continuous runtime governance, with a required minimum evidence package for higher-risk devices.
Calls the framework a useful start and wants explicit modifiers: autonomy and privilege, reversibility, traceability, detectability, changeability and downstream safeguards.
Says patient-facing status should not proxy risk; what matters is whether users can review the basis, certainty is warranted, time allows checks and actions follow.
Wants risk assessed over full conversational and action trajectories, testing equivalent prompts, contradictions, long-context decay and bypass attempts.
Wants under- and over-escalation reported separately, since their harms, thresholds and tradeoffs are not interchangeable.
Calls the framework sound but not a one-time exam; results matter only if the tested configuration is deployed, controlled and enforceable at runtime.
Would require acceptance criteria at outcome, process and control levels, including whether unsafe actions can be observed, recorded and stopped.
Says public benchmarks cannot be the sole gate; construct validity means linking benchmarks to use, users, environment and failure modes, independence rising with risk.
Accepts synthetic data for rare, adversarial and coverage tests if reported separately, with generator, protocol, independence and subgroup coverage disclosed.
Supports third parties for sequestered data and adjudication, with competence, conflicts disclosure, reproducibility and evidence portability to avoid lock-in.
Allows more postmarket reliance only with bounded uncertainty, containable harm and timely monitoring, never where autonomous action could cause irreversible harm.
Says cadence alone is insufficient; wants event-triggered reassessment on component changes, threshold breaches, new failure modes, context changes and configuration drift.
Wants postmarket evidence traceable from requirement to control, version, trigger, decision and corrective action, using machine-readable policies.
Says supervisory agents can help at machine speed but are not reliable just for using a different model; their authority, inputs and changes need validation.
Lists design expectations: architectural separation, deterministic enforcement of clear prohibitions, independent failure testing, fail-safe behavior, tamper-evident logs, escalation paths.
Would treat a supervisory agent as a safety-relevant component whenever the device relies on it for reasonable assurance.
Sees master files cutting duplicative review if specific enough, listing versioning, excluded uses, failure modes, subgroup results, rollback and notification commitments.
Says voluntary files will not suffice without incentives; suggests supplier contracts, change-notice minimums, version manifests and sponsor verification tests, with manufacturers accountable.
Says agents can turn a reasoning error into real actions before anyone intervenes, so evaluation should cover the whole plan-action-observation loop.
Wants a record of agent identity and authority binding each agent to owner, authorized tools, permissions, versions and revocation status, with tool calls attributable.
Expects least privilege, allowlisted tools, pre-action policy checks, human approval before irreversible acts, rollback, injection resistance and a testable kill switch.
Wants acceptance criteria beyond task success: prohibited-action and unauthorized-tool rates, checkpoint adherence, tool-failure recovery and time to containment.
Proposes a risk-scaled minimum runtime governance evidence package, from requirement maps and deployed configuration to runtime decisions, drift and tested fail-safes.
Calls the paper a timely foundation whose lifecycle view should be made operational, governing consequential actions before execution rather than after incidents.
